# Multifactor Screen Review — S&P 500 Top 10
### Preliminary note on methodology

These ten names are the current top decile of a five-factor percentile ranking (value 30% · quality 25% · growth 15% · momentum 15% · expectativas 15%) run across the full S&P 500. A score of 75 means "75th percentile of the index this week" — it is relative, not absolute, and it will shift as other constituents' fundamentals and prices move. No factor score here should be read as a valuation call ("cheap"/"expensive") on its own, and nothing in this report is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold.

Two flags recur through the list and materially change how much weight each score deserves:

- **`beneficio_en_pico = true`** (earnings at a cyclical high relative to the multi-year normalized base): seven of ten names carry this flag. In every one of these cases, the gap between trailing PER and `per_normalizado` is large — the stock looks statistically cheap on trailing earnings precisely because trailing earnings are elevated. This is the classic trap the brief warns about.
- **`cobertura_pct` below ~90%**: only SYF (50%) and IBKR (75%) fall meaningfully short of full data coverage. Their scores — especially the value and quality legs — rest on partial inputs (missing leverage, cash-flow-conversion and interest-coverage data) and should be treated as less robust than the others.

---

## Company-by-company

**1. ACGL — Arch Capital Group (score 75.6)**
Broad-based score: value (94.6), growth (79.3) and expectativas (83.3) are all strong, quality (65.8) is solidly above median, and the only weak leg is momentum (42.3) — the stock is trading below both its 50- and 200-day averages with an RSI near 37 (oversold territory). Notably, `beneficio_en_pico` is **false** here, and coverage is full (94%), which makes this the most fundamentally grounded score in the group: the value read isn't an artifact of a temporary earnings spike (normalized PER 8.96 is actually close to trailing PER 7.52). The one caution from public reporting: recent commentary flags a projected quarterly earnings decline and pressure from catastrophe losses and softer premium pricing — consistent with why the market (momentum) hasn't yet endorsed the story. Four of five factors agree; the market is the outlier, which cuts both ways.

**2. NEM — Newmont Corporation (score 75.4)**
Driven almost entirely by growth (98.2), quality (81.2) and momentum (80.7); value is only middling (56.4) and there is no expectativas reading at all (null), so the reverse-DCF check that exists for most peers is simply unavailable here — a real gap in the picture. `beneficio_en_pico` is **true**, and the scale of the distortion is the largest in the list: normalized profit growth of ~6,985% and a normalized PER of 72x versus a trailing PER of 16x both point to earnings — and the multi-year base against which they're compared — being unusually depressed historically and now running very hot, almost certainly tracking the gold price rather than a structural change in the business. Momentum is real (price is 16% above its 200-day average, +61% over 12 months) but that agreement is itself a commodity-cycle signal, not independent confirmation.

**3. TRV — The Travelers Companies (score 73.6)**
Four of five factors are strong (value 83.4, growth 76.3, momentum 82.8, expectativas 58.3 — the latter more moderate than most peers, meaning less of a valuation cushion is priced against delivered growth); quality is mid-pack (63.8). `beneficio_en_pico` is **true** and the trailing-vs-normalized PER gap (10.1x vs 18.3x) is wide, so the "cheap" trailing multiple should be discounted. Coverage is full. Sell-side commentary found is lukewarm — a consensus "Hold" with average price targets roughly in line with or slightly below the current quote — which sits awkwardly next to the strong momentum score and is worth noting as a check on enthusiasm.

**4. SYF — Synchrony Financial (score 73.5)**
Only two of five factors are genuinely strong: value (89.5) and expectativas (91.7, the second-highest in the group). Growth (54.2) and momentum (53.8) are unremarkable, and quality (66.6) is built on an incomplete data set. **Coverage is 50%** — leverage, free-cash-flow, EV/EBIT, ROIC and interest-coverage fields are all missing, which for a consumer-credit lender are precisely the metrics that matter most for judging credit quality and balance-sheet risk. `beneficio_en_pico` is true, though the normalized-vs-trailing PER gap (8.0x vs 7.8x) is small, so the peak-earnings distortion looks less severe here than for TRV or NEM. No independent news was found to corroborate or challenge the picture. This is a score built on a narrower and less complete base than its rank suggests.

**5. INCY — Incyte Corporation (score 73.4)**
Growth (93.1), momentum (84.2) and quality (77.2) are strong; value is only middling (55.0), and there is no expectativas reading (null). `beneficio_en_pico` is **true**, with the widest normalized-growth number in the list after Newmont/Allstate context (297.6% normalized profit growth) and a large trailing-to-normalized PER gap (15.5x vs 43.6x) — consistent with lumpy, milestone- or royalty-driven biotech earnings rather than a steady operating trend. Balance sheet metrics (very high interest coverage, low leverage) are genuinely strong and not in question. But with no expectativas check available, there's no read on how much of this growth the market has already priced in.

**6. APA — APA Corporation (score 72.7)**
Value (90.2), quality (77.8) and momentum (92.3, the highest in the group) are all strong, but growth is the outlier at just 9.6 — normalized profit growth is actually **negative** (-40.8%) and normalized revenue growth is negative too (-8.0%). `beneficio_en_pico` is **false** — the opposite problem from most peers: current earnings sit below the multi-year normalized base. The result is an unusual disconnect: the stock is up 101% over twelve months and trading 33% above its 200-day average while its own normalized fundamentals are declining. That gap between price action and multi-year fundamentals is the largest in the group and deserves more scrutiny than the headline score conveys.

**7. IBKR — Interactive Brokers Group (score 72.3)**
Growth (88.5), momentum (86.0) and expectativas (100.0, the maximum score in the index) stand out; value (43.3) is only average and quality (72.4) is solid but not exceptional. Coverage is 75% — several cash-flow and leverage metrics are missing. `beneficio_en_pico` is **true**, and the scale of the effect is extreme: a normalized PER of 229x against a trailing PER of 36x implies the normalized earnings base is very thin relative to current profits, likely reflecting genuine business scaling (rate-driven interest income, trading-volume growth — both mentioned in recent coverage) rather than a one-off. That same thin denominator, however, is exactly what can produce an artificially perfect expectativas score of 100 — this reading should be treated as a statistical artifact of rapid earnings scaling rather than a straightforward "market underestimates this business" signal. The elevated debt-to-equity figure (205.7%) is also less comparable here than for other constituents, given IBKR's brokerage/margin-lending balance sheet structure.

**8. HIG — The Hartford Insurance Group (score 72.1)**
A profile close to ACGL's: value (90.1), growth (71.6) and expectativas (75.0) are strong, quality (65.4) is mid-pack, and momentum (44.6) is the weak leg — price is barely above its 200-day average and 6-/12-month returns are close to flat. Unlike ACGL, however, `beneficio_en_pico` is **true** here, with a meaningful trailing-to-normalized PER gap (9.4x vs 13.1x), so the value score carries a bit more peak-earnings risk than ACGL's equivalent read. Coverage is full.

**9. AIZ — Assurant, Inc. (score 72.0)**
Value (79.7), growth (71.6) and momentum (81.9) are solid; quality is the weakest link in the group among fully-covered names (57.0), reflecting a lower ROA (2.56%) and the lowest operating margin (9.3%) of the ten. There is no expectativas reading (null). `beneficio_en_pico` is **true**, with a wide trailing-to-normalized PER gap (13.5x vs 21.8x). Public commentary found described a year-to-date price gain and some analyst optimism, but this could not be verified beyond a brief snippet and should not be treated as confirmed detail.

**10. ALL — Allstate Corporation (score 71.5)**
The broadest score on paper — value (86.6), growth (83.4) and momentum (78.2) all strong, quality (65.3) middling — but expectativas is the lowest reading of any name with a valid score (33.3), meaning the market's current price already embeds comparatively demanding growth assumptions relative to what has actually been delivered on a normalized basis. This sits alongside the single most extreme peak-earnings signature in the group: normalized profit growth of 866.96% and a trailing PER of just 5.1x against a normalized PER of 19.1x. Both numbers point the same way — a business recovering sharply off a depressed multi-year base (consistent with a prior period of adverse auto-insurance underwriting results), where the current trailing multiple looks cheapest exactly when the underlying earnings are least representative of a normal year. `beneficio_en_pico` is true and coverage is full, so this isn't a data problem — it's a genuine base-effect distortion sitting underneath an otherwise attractive-looking score.

---

## Closing ranking by conviction

The score order and the conviction order are not the same. Reordering reflects (a) how many of the five factors are independently corroborating the story, (b) whether a `beneficio_en_pico` flag is paired with a large trailing/normalized PER gap (bigger gap = more of the "cheapness" is a peak-earnings mirage), and (c) data completeness.

| Conviction rank | Ticker | Score rank | Why it moved (or didn't) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ACGL | 1 | Only constituent with `beneficio_en_pico = false`, full coverage, four of five factors strong; weak momentum is the market's problem to resolve, not a data problem. |
| 2 | TRV | 3 | Broad-based and momentum agrees, but the trailing/normalized PER gap is real — some of the "value" is peak-earnings driven. |
| 3 | HIG | 8 | Structurally similar to ACGL but carries the peak-earnings flag with a meaningful PER gap and weaker momentum; moved up modestly only because four of five factors are still genuinely strong. |
| 4 | AIZ | 9 | Reasonably broad, but quality is the visible weak point and there's no expectativas check to confirm the pricing hasn't run ahead of fundamentals. |
| 5 | IBKR | 7 | Growth/momentum look fundamentally supported by known business drivers, but the expectativas score of 100 likely reflects a statistical artifact of an extremely thin normalized-earnings base rather than a clean mispricing signal; coverage also incomplete. |
| 6 | NEM | 2 | Score rests heavily on growth, quality and momentum that all trace back to the gold price; the largest normalized-growth distortion in the list and no expectativas read to sanity-check it. Dropped despite the second-highest score. |
| 7 | INCY | 5 | Same base-effect concern as NEM (large one-off-looking normalized profit growth) plus no expectativas read; balance-sheet quality is genuine, but the growth number should not be extrapolated. |
| 8 | SYF | 4 | Only 50% data coverage — the score is built on missing leverage and cash-flow data for a lender, where those are exactly the metrics that matter. Dropped from #4 to #8 on data-quality grounds alone. |
| 9 | APA | 6 | Largest fundamentals/price disconnect in the group: momentum near the top of the index while normalized growth is outright negative. |
| 10 | ALL | 10 | Lowest expectativas score in the set and the most extreme trailing-vs-normalized PER gap — the clearest textbook case of a cyclical looking cheapest exactly when it is priciest. |

**Read on the disagreements:** the biggest downgrades from score order go to NEM and SYF — NEM because its strength is concentrated in factors that are plausibly one commodity cycle, not four independent signals, and it lacks an expectations check; SYF because its score is simply built on half the usual data. The biggest relative upgrade is ACGL, precisely because it is the one name in the top ten that is *not* flagged as sitting on peak earnings and has complete data behind every factor.

This is a research summary of factor construction and publicly available context, not a valuation judgment or trading recommendation.

methodology.approach: Factor scoring, not threshold filtering. Every company in the index is ranked against every other on each metric, and the ranks are combined with the weights below. Nothing is rejected for scoring poorly — only for being impossible to evaluate.
methodology.why_not_filters: A hard filter chain (ROE > 20% AND P/E < 20 AND ...) discards a company at 19.8% ROE as readily as one at 3%, empties the screen when no name clears every bar, throws away how far each company cleared or missed, and silently gives RSI the same weight as ROE. A cross-sectional rank has none of those problems.
methodology.why_ranks_not_values: Scores are built from percentile ranks rather than raw values. One company emerging from a cyclical trough at +1,368% earnings growth would otherwise dominate any average and turn a multi-factor score into a single column in disguise. A rank treats that as what it is — first place — and nothing more.

value.what_it_measures: What you pay for what the business earns and owns. Built on normalised earnings rather than the last twelve months, so a company at the top of its cycle does not read as cheap.

quality.what_it_measures: Whether the business earns its returns on real capital and turns profit into cash. Accruals and leverage sit here because both are ways a good-looking profit can fail to be one.

growth.what_it_measures: How fast revenue and earnings are compounding, measured against a multi-year base rather than a single prior year — a comparison against one weak year is arithmetic, not growth.

momentum.what_it_measures: Whether the price agrees. Deliberately the lowest weight in the value screens: a company that has fallen is cheaper, not worse, and momentum should not be able to veto it.

expectativas.what_it_measures: How much growth today's price already demands, from the reverse DCF, against what the business has actually delivered. It is the only factor that scores the market's expectations rather than the company.

methodology.missing_data: A metric a company does not report scores nothing — never zero. Scoring a gap as the worst possible value punishes a company for a data provider's omission, and that is the kind of error that never appears in the table and decides the order anyway. A factor is averaged over the metrics that exist, and the weights are renormalised over the factors that exist.
methodology.coverage: Because weights renormalise, a company with thin data scores as confidently as a complete one. cobertura_pct is published alongside every score for exactly that reason: 90 on 40% coverage is an opinion about very little.
methodology.what_the_score_is_not: The score is a position within this index, not a grade and not a valuation. A company's score moves when other companies move. It says nothing about whether the name is worth owning, and it is not a recommendation.
methodology.read_the_breakdown: The per-factor scores matter more than the total. 'Cheap and high quality but no momentum' is a statement you can argue with; a composite of 67 is not.
methodology.two_stage: Four factors are ranked across the whole index (500 companies). The fifth, expectativas, comes from a reverse DCF that reads SEC filings and cannot run at that scale, so the top 25 are valued and ranked on it among themselves. The other four keep their index-wide percentile — re-ranking them inside an already-selected group would measure something different and read as if it did not.
methodology.report_size: The 10 highest-scoring companies go into the written report. That number is chosen rather than whatever a threshold happened to admit, which is what makes the cost of the run predictable.

valuation_method.model: Two-stage DCF on levered free cash flow (FCF discounted at cost of equity, compared with market cap — no net-debt bridge)
valuation_method.discount_rate: CAPM: currency-matched risk-free rate + beta x 5% ERP, beta clamped to [0.3, 2.5], rate clamped to [5%, 18%]. Only USD has a live quote (^TNX); other currencies use a documented static rate, flagged per company in risk_free_source.
valuation_method.implied_growth: Reverse DCF — the FCF growth rate that sets the model's equity value equal to today's market cap. What the price assumes, not a forecast. Available for every company, since it needs no history.
valuation_method.trend_test: A projection is only made when a least-squares line through log FCF reaches R2 >= 0.5. Below that the series is a path rather than a direction, dcf_value_per_share is null and dcf_skipped_reason says so.
valuation_method.probability: P(growth >= implied growth) under a Student-t fitted to the company's own year-on-year FCF growth in log space. Withheld entirely above a log stdev of 1.0, where it would be indistinguishable from a coin flip.
known_limits: History depth is uneven. SEC filings give US companies 14-17 years (16 growth observations for Adobe), but that source only covers SEC filers, so the IBEX screener and any company whose filing history has gaps falls back to yfinance's 4 years — 3 observations. Each company's fcf_source and probability.observations say which it got, and every probability is published as a range rather than a point.

A short FCF window can catch a trough, a spike or both and mistake it for a trend, and a long one can fit an earlier version of the company beautifully. The R2 test guards the first, and projecting the lower of the long-run and recent trends guards the second. Neither is a cure.
Terminal growth is a single 2.5% applied to every business regardless of its long-run ceiling; dcf_terminal_value_share_pct shows how much of each valuation rests on it.

The model sees free cash flow only — no revenue detail, margins, guidance or segments. A one-off legal settlement, licensing payment or deferred capex is indistinguishable from a genuine trend change, which is why revenue growth is carried alongside as a corroboration check.
Levered FCF is compared directly against market cap with no net-debt bridge — a deliberate simplification for data robustness across 500 tickers.

# What the Market Is Paying For: A Reverse-DCF Reading of 25 S&P 500 Names

The only number every company here shares is `implied_growth_pct` — the FCF growth rate that today's market cap already assumes, discounted at each company's own CAPM cost of equity. Everything else (trend fit, historical CAGR, probability) either supports that number, contradicts it, or — as often happens — cannot speak to it at all because the cash-flow history is not trend-like. I split the set into companies whose FCF history clears the `trend_r2 ≥ 0.5` bar (a projection is at least defensible) and those where it doesn't (only the implied growth figure survives).

---

## Group A — Cash flows behave like a trend (`trend_r2 ≥ 0.5`)

For these fourteen names, `gap_pp` (implied growth minus trend growth) is real evidence, not arithmetic on noise.

| Ticker | Implied growth | Trend r² | Trend growth | Gap (pp) | DCF upside | TV share | Prob. range (obs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ALL | **-11.0%** (shrink) | 0.56, but trend broken | 6.2% | -17.2 | +309.6% | 71.8% | 66.1–72.5% (n=16) |
| TRV | **-9.2%** (shrink) | 0.999 | 17.9% | -27.1 | +757.7% | 76.2% | 99.8–100% (n=3) |
| ACGL | **-17.1%** (shrink) | 0.895 | 18.3% | -35.4 | +1,636.6% | 79.8% | 89.1–96.2% (n=14) |
| CINF | **-6.1%** (shrink) | 0.878 | 13.7% | -19.8 | +322.7% | 70.3% | 67.0–73.9% (n=15) |
| PGR | **-10.4%** (shrink) | 0.939, trend broken | 18.0% | -28.4 | +911.8% | 79.7% | 86.3–93.9% (n=16) |
| HIG | **-11.6%** (shrink) | 0.839 | 17.1% | -28.8 | +871.4% | 75.8% | 76.1–93.9% (n=3) |
| SYF | **-21.7%** (shrink) | 0.843 | 13.8% | -35.5 | +860.4% | 55.5% | 90.8–98.7% (n=3) |
| WRB | **-12.0%** (shrink) | 0.82 | 12.0% | -24.0 | +609.6% | 76.2% | 81.4–96.2% (n=3) |
| FSLR | null — *above the model's range* | 0.608 | 11.2% | n/a | -97.7% | 45.4% | not estimable |
| HPQ | **+0.9%** (near flat) | 0.62 | -7.4% | +8.3 | -63.8% | 21.6% | 37.8–41.6% (n=15) |
| ADBE | **+4.4%** (slower growth) | 0.93 | 18.0% | -13.6 | +29.1% | 47.6% | 67.2–73.9% (n=16) |
| GL | **-7.3%** (shrink) | 0.677 | 3.0% | -10.3 | +44.9% | 57.1% | 72.2–80.1% (n=16) |
| MCK | **+0.2%** (flat) | 0.829 | 5.6% | -5.4 | +55.9% | 71.1% | 61.0–65.6% (n=16) |
| IBKR | **+7.9%** (growth) | 0.945 | 62.3% | -54.4 | DCF declined | — | 77.3–94.5% (n=3) |

**Reading these:** In every insurance name (ALL, TRV, ACGL, CINF, PGR, HIG, SYF, WRB) the implied growth is *negative* — the price already assumes free cash flow shrinks from here, sometimes by more than 20% a year — even though the company's own trend line, fit with r² of 0.82–1.0, has been running at double-digit *growth*. The gap is consistently 17–36 percentage points below trend. That is not a claim the stocks are "cheap"; it is a statement that the price embeds a much harsher path than the recent, well-fitted trend. Whether that trend continues is unknowable from this data — insurance FCF is famously lumpy with reserve and underwriting cycles — but the gap itself is real, not an artifact of a poor-fitting line.

Two of these (ALL, PGR) carry a caveat: `trend_broken=true`, meaning the most recent year's growth (23% and 28% respectively) has run well above the multi-year trend line even though the overall r² still clears 0.5. The trend fit is statistically real but recent behavior is accelerating away from it — worth flagging, not smoothing over.

ADBE, GL, MCK sit closer to flat-to-slow-growth pricing, with smaller negative gaps (-5 to -14pp) — the market's assumption diverges from trend by less here than in the insurers.

HPQ is the one positive-gap case: the price (implied +0.9%) actually assumes *less* decline than the trend line (-7.4%) or the more recent trend (-14.9%, used as the model's growth input) would suggest. The market is pricing a stabilization that the trend itself doesn't show yet.

**FSLR is a genuine oddity.** The reverse DCF could not even be run — `implied_growth_status: above_model_range` means the growth rate needed to justify FSLR's market cap exceeds what the model's growth band can express at all. Separately, the *forward* DCF (built off the 11.2% trend growth, which does clear the r² bar) produces a fair value of $4.78 against a $209.03 price — a -97.7% "upside." Two consistent messages from one incompatible pair of numbers: the price requires a growth rate the model cannot even state, while the fitted historical trend, taken at face value, says the shares are worth a small fraction of the price. Both outputs came from the same cash-flow series; neither should be read as a forecast.

**IBKR is a different kind of caution.** The trend fit is excellent (r²=0.945) but the trend itself is 62.3% annual FCF growth — a number the model treats as too extreme to build a terminal value around, so `dcf_value_per_share` is null by design, not by omission. The reverse DCF still produced an implied growth of 7.9%, well below that trend, but no forward valuation exists to compare it to responsibly.

Discount-rate note: ALL, ACGL, PGR, WRB, and EG (Group B) all have `beta_clamped=true` — their own reported betas were lower than the model's floor, so the discount rate does not reflect the raw beta. SYF, PYPL, HPQ, ADBE, TROW, IBKR, DAL sit at the high end (β > 1.2), pushing their cost of equity toward 11–12%.

---

## Group B — Cash flows do not behave like a trend (`trend_r2 < 0.5`)

For these eleven companies, no projection was attempted — the least-squares fit through the FCF history explains too little of the variance to call it a direction. The honest output is the implied growth number alone, with the reason nothing further can be said.

| Ticker | Implied growth | r² | Revenue growth | FCF-vs-rev divergence | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NEM | **+11.1%** (growth priced in) | 0.047 | 23.9% | -19.4pp | no usable estimate (log stdev 1.39 > 1.0) |
| INCY | **+13.3%** (growth priced in) | 0.009 | 14.8% | -9.2pp | no usable estimate (1.39) |
| APA | **-3.7%** (shrink priced in) | 0.057 | -6.96% | -4.0pp | no usable estimate (1.06) |
| AIZ | **-4.5%** (shrink priced in) | 0.167 | 7.9% | -0.4pp | 56.5–59.4% (n=16) |
| PYPL | **-2.3%** (shrink priced in) | 0.231 | 6.4% | +1.1pp | 53.1–59.3% (n=3) |
| CB | **-8.8%** (shrink priced in) | 0.292 | 11.6% | -5.0pp | 62.4–80.5% (n=3) |
| TROW | **+11.1%** (growth priced in) | 0.081 | 4.1% | +3.5pp | no usable estimate (1.45) |
| SNDK | **+23.95%** (growth priced in) | null | 49.3% | null | no usable estimate (0 obs, fewer than 2 YoY points) |
| DAL | **+10.5%** (growth priced in) | 0.039 | 7.8% | -15.0pp | 55.9–60.2% (n=8) |
| EG | **-23.5%** (shrink priced in) | 0.08 | 12.8% | -17.5pp | 62.8–81.1% (n=3) |
| MRK | **+3.0%** (growth priced in) | 0.251 | 3.1% | +2.0pp | 54.8–56.9% (n=16) |

Nothing here should be read as "the trend growth was X%" — there is no trend to quote. What can be said is only the implied growth (what the price needs) and, where it corroborates or contradicts, the revenue growth line. NEM and INCY show implied growth well below revenue growth (-19.4pp and -9.2pp), meaning FCF has been growing off a lower base or with more volatility than the top line — consistent with capex timing or working-capital swings in a miner and a biotech respectively, though this data cannot say which. SNDK is a special case: only four FCF data points, three of them near-zero or negative, followed by an $11.5bn print — too short and too discontinuous to fit anything, and even the probability model could not produce two usable year-on-year growth observations.

---

## Reading the probability figures

`probability.probability_pct` answers a narrow question: in this company's own log-growth history, how often did growth clear the rate the market is now pricing in? A high band (TRV, 99.8–100%; ACGL, 89–96%; SYF, 91–99%) means the company's own past almost always beat today's implied bar — largely because the implied growth is deeply negative and the historical series has rarely been negative. That says the bar is low relative to history, not that the future will clear it. A low band (HPQ, 38–42%; MRK, 55–57%) says the reverse: the implied bar has historically been cleared less than half the time. Where `probability_pct` is null (NEM, INCY, APA, TROW, SNDK), that is not "no data" being swept aside — it is the model refusing to fit a Student-t distribution to a series whose log-standard-deviation exceeds 1.0, because at that level of dispersion a probability figure would be noise dressed as precision.

Sample size matters here more than the point estimate does. Companies drawing on the full 13–17 year XBRL history (ALL, ACGL, CINF, PGR, GL, MCK, MRK, AIZ, TROW) have 14–16 observations behind their probability — thin by any normal statistical standard, but meaningfully thicker than the 3-observation estimates built only on 4 years of reported FCF (TRV, HIG, SYF, WRB, CB, EG, PYPL, IBKR). For those, the quoted range is wide precisely because three data points cannot pin down a distribution's tails — treat the range, not the midpoint, as the finding.

---

## Where this model is most likely to be wrong

- **Three observations, one distribution.** Roughly half the companies here (TRV, HIG, SYF, WRB, CB, EG, PYPL, IBKR, and the null case SNDK) rest their probability estimate on just three year-on-year growth figures. A Student-t fit on three points has enormous parameter uncertainty; the quoted range already reflects that, but the range itself should be read as "wide and soft," not as a calibrated confidence interval.

- **A four-year FCF window on cyclical businesses.** Where `fcf_source` is "Free Cash Flow (reported)" with `fcf_years: 4`, the entire read — trend, historical CAGR, probability — comes from one recent slice of a cycle. IBKR's 62% trend growth is almost certainly a trading-volume and rate-cycle artifact, not a sustainable FCF growth rate, which is exactly why the model refused to build a terminal value on it. Insurers with only four years on file (TRV, HIG, SYF, WRB, CB, EG) could easily be sitting on the up-leg of an underwriting cycle that a four-year window cannot distinguish from a genuine structural trend. Delta's own series shows why this matters more broadly: a 13-year window that includes a -$5.7bn pandemic year and near-zero prints either side of it, followed by a recovery, produces an r² of 0.039 — the model correctly refuses to call that a trend, but a shorter window landing only on the recovery years could have manufactured false confidence.

- **One terminal growth rate for every business.** Every completed DCF here uses the same 2.5% perpetual growth rate after year 10, and for most names the terminal value is 55–80% of the entire equity value (ACGL 79.8%, PGR 79.7%, HIG 75.8%, TRV 76.2%, WRB 76.2%). That means the bulk of these valuations is not really about the explicit ten-year forecast at all — it is about whether a miner (NEM, not run), an insurer, and a software company (ADBE) all deserve the identical long-run growth ceiling. They plainly do not have the same long-run reinvestment opportunity, competitive durability, or capital intensity, and the model has no mechanism to tell them apart on that dimension.

- **Cash flow with no memory of its cause.** The model sees a number, never the reason for it. A one-off legal settlement, an insurance reserve release, a licensing payment, or a deferred capex program all show up as "FCF growth" indistinguishable from an operating improvement. FSLR's history of alternating multi-hundred-million-dollar negative and positive years, NEM's 2021 near-zero print followed by a jump to $7.3bn, and AIZ's 2015–2016 collapse to under $150m before recovering are all consistent with this: the series moves, but nothing here says whether the move was organic. That is precisely why low-r² names were not projected, and why even the trend-supported names should be read as "cash flow moved this way," not "the business is on this path."
